Insane study on how AI agents choose products 🤯

So now we know how to trick AI agents into buying your thing:

1/ AI agents almost always choose the cheaper product
->  Asked "Dyson or Shark?", they picked the Shark 91% of the time, because it does nearly the same job for a third of the price

2/ Grok Bot uses the app it's connected to, even when it thinks another app is better
->  It said Adobe Podcast was the best tool for cleaning up audio, then used Descript anyway because Descript is connected to Grok

3/ "Only 3 left in stock" has zero effect on AI shoppers
->  Agents ignored urgency tricks built for people, so fake scarcity won't sell to them

4/ AI agents don't care how famous your brand is
->  Across 1,186 picks, the brand name almost never came up as a reason for choosing a product

5/ Luxury doesn't sell to AI either
->  Asked to pick a birthday gift, agents chose the cheaper Shark over the Dyson 7 out of 8 times

6/ Discounts don't work the way you think
->  Under 10% off didn't change a single pick, and over 50% off looked too good to be true, so agents avoided the deal

7/ A small company with honest pricing can beat a giant
->  Porkbun sells far fewer domains than GoDaddy, yet it ranks #9 for purchases made by AI agents and GoDaddy ranks #112, because Porkbun's price stays the same every year

8/ Meta's Muse mostly recommends products from the Facebook and Instagram catalog
->  It almost always starts there and pulls only 50 options, so if your products aren't in that catalog it likely never sees you

9/ Forcing people to log in kills AI sales
->  With guest checkout, agents reached the end of the form in 81% of runs, and a required account stopped every single one

10/ Expensive products win only when the shopper names a specific need
->  When the shopper said "I'll use it every day", agents switched from the Shark to the pricier Dyson 7 out of 8 times

11/ A better return policy wins the sale
->  When two stores had the same price, agents picked the one with better returns 86% of the time

Prepared by a growth hacker from Ryze AI, the AI marketing engineer

🌶️ take: between model jaggedness and usage limits, AI lab subscriptions are going to start making less and less sense.

Here's what I mean.

Gemini Neon is crushing it, and people love it. It especially excels at communicating and writing.

But IMO other models like Fable or Opus are still better at particular things like design.

But there are tons of people talking about now switching to using Gemini or Antigravity apps via subscription, basically shifting their entire workflow to a new tool because that's the new hot model.

We have no idea what other model will come out next week from which lab that we will love for which tasks.

In order to consistently use the best model from the big labs you would need roughly $800 a month worth of subs (assuming max plans) and that's if you only have one of each, which many people don't due to usage limits.

You also need an effective orchestrator tool and process to manage those.

Or, what I'm doing now, you can install something like the @OpenRouter MCP into your agent of choice, Grok Bot for me, and use it to orchestrate specific workflows with specific models.

This is what I'm doing now and it works pretty well but I think a better model is a harness/tool with two layers: one is a general agent/chat layer, similar to what we have now.

And the other is a workflow layer where you have defined, semi-deterministic workflows that chain together different models to complete and end-to-end task. Similar to skills but more deterministic and structured.

We are getting to the point now where we have enough neurodiversity in our models that we can effectively build things like this using usage-based pricing at a comparable or smaller cost than stacking multiple subscriptions.

This is only going to continue to be more true as intelligent routing like our autorouter continue to improve.

Btw if this is interesting to you, you should definitely sign up for the waitlist for Ori: https://t.co/C5vEjS2mCv
